newsitem.title: UK: UK retailers reassure consumers on gene foods.
newsitem.headline: UK retailers reassure consumers on gene foods.

text.p: UK food retailers moved to reassure customers over genetically modified (GM) foods on Thursday after Britain's Consumer Association said consumers were being denied the choice of whether or not to buy such products.
Tesco, Britain's leading food retailer, said it would label genetically modified foods, despite the problems created by the lack of a separate chain of supply for GM material.
This policy would compel suppliers to segregate ingredients like soy and maize into modified and unmodified groups, the company said in a statement.
The products involved so far are a type of gene-modified soy developed by Monsanto Co in the U.S., and a gene maize produced by Swiss chemicals group Ciba Geigy AG.
European environmental groups oppose genetically altered foods, claiming that they may pose health risks.
Tesco had introduced leaflets explaining the issues, and was making available to its customers a list of products free of soy and another of those containing no genetically modified ingredients.
The chain had acquired stocks of unmodified soy to supply its bakeries, and none of its breakfast cereals contained modified maize, it said.
On December 13, Tesco announced that it was banning unprocessed genetically modified maize from animal feed within its producer group.

"Generally we support the introduction of genetically engineered foodstuff, where there are definite consumer benefits and when they have been judged safe by the relevant government organisations," Tesco said.

Where the use of modified material was positively identified, the product would be labelled, retailer Safeway Plc said in a statement responding to a report in the Consumer Association's "Which?" magazine.
Where the presence of GM material could not be positively identified, Safeway would provide information to customers through explanatory leaflets and product listings.

"With regards to imported GM commodity crops like soya or maize, we recognise that any requirement for traceability can only be guaranteed through segregation of the processed ingredient," Safeway said.
A spokesman for the group told Reuters that Safeway, like Tesco, had ensured a supply of unmodified soy for its bakeries for this year.

Marks & Spencer plc said in a statement that "individual labelling may not be possible in the case of foods containing ingredients derived from commodity crops imported from abroad such as soya where these are not segregated after leaving the farm."
In such cases information would be available to consumers identifying products that might contain those ingredients, Marks & Spencer said.
